chapter.title: Lying on the bed: floating

cards.body: The hardest part of floating is doing nothing at all. Your lungs are two air bags built into your chest, and **the water is a bed waiting under them**. Today you lie down on it, back first, then front, and let it take your weight.
cards.simpler: The hardest part of floating is doing nothing at all. Your lungs are like two air bags inside your chest, and **the water is a bed waiting under them**. Today you lie down on that bed. First on your back, then on your front. Your only job is to let the water hold your weight.

cards.prompt: Priya lies back in the shallow end with a huge breath held in, floating nicely. Then she lets the whole lot out in one long, dramatic sigh. What happens next?

options.text: She floats higher, now that she's relaxed
Her hips and legs start to sink
Nothing changes: air has nothing to do with floating

whyNot.a: That's relaxing her muscles, not emptying her lungs: loose is good, but the sigh let out the air that was holding her up.
whyNot.c: That's the floor idea, not the bed idea: the air in her chest is exactly what was keeping it at the surface.

cards.reteach: Think of a beach ball tucked inside your ribs. Full, it bobs at the top. Let the air out and it rides lower, and your chest does the same every time you breathe out hard.

cards.title: The air bags
cards.body:
A full breath works like **a beach ball tucked inside your ribs**. Breathe in all the way and your chest rides at the surface. Sigh it all out and you sink a few centimetres, sometimes more.

On your back, your head and hips sit on a seesaw. Lift your head to look at your toes and your hips go down. Lay your ears in the water, look at the ceiling, and your hips come up.

So: ears in, chin pointing at the roof, belly button lifted. Take small sips of air near the top of a full breath. Never empty the ball.
cards.simpler: A full breath is like **a beach ball tucked inside your ribs**. Breathe in fully and your chest stays at the surface. Breathe it all out and you sink a few centimetres, sometimes more. On your back, your head and hips are a seesaw. Lift your head and your hips drop. Rest your ears in the water, look up, and your hips rise. Keep your belly button lifted. Sip small breaths near the top. Never empty the ball.

cards.title: Tom counts the ceiling
cards.body: Tom, 34, holds the pool edge with both hands and lies back, staring at the lights. Ears in, belly button up, one big breath held near the top. He lets go with one hand, then the other, and counts 22 ceiling tiles before he remembers he was supposed to be nervous. His feet drift down until they hang a hand's width below the surface, and stop there. **That's not sinking; that's floating.**
cards.simpler: Tom, 34, holds the pool edge with both hands and lies back, looking up at the lights. Ears in, belly button up, one big breath held near the top. He lets go with one hand, then the other. He counts 22 ceiling tiles before he remembers to feel nervous. His feet drift down until they hang a hand's width below the surface, then stop. **That's not sinking; that's floating.**

cards.prompt: You're on your back, hands off the wall, and your hips keep slowly dropping. Which fix uses what you just learned?

options.text: Lift your head to check what your legs are doing
Lay your ears back in the water and top up your breath
Breathe all the way out so your body goes heavy and calm

whyNot.a: That's the seesaw the wrong way round, not a fix: head up pushes hips down.
whyNot.c: That's emptying the beach ball, not relaxing: less air means a lower chest and lower hips.

cards.reteach: Two things lift your hips on your back: a head that rests in the water and lungs that stay mostly full. Lifting your head or sighing out does the opposite. Head back, breath in, then wait.

cards.title: Face down, and getting up
cards.body:
The front float is the same bed, face down. Hold the wall, take a full breath, face in, and let your legs drift up behind you. Let go, arms out like a starfish, and count to 10, letting out **a slow thread of bubbles, not the whole breath**.

You'd think standing up from your back is the scary part. It's chapter 1's move with your chin leading: chin to chest, knees in, hands press down, feet on the floor.

Some legs hang low no matter what. Normal. Your chest still floats.
cards.simpler: The front float is the same bed, face down. Hold the wall, take a full breath, face in, and let your legs drift up. Let go, arms out like a starfish, and count to 10, letting out **a slow thread of bubbles, not the whole breath**. Getting up from your back is chapter 1's move, chin first: chin to chest, knees in, hands press down, feet on the floor. Some legs hang low anyway. That's normal. Your chest still floats.

cards.body: Sam floats on his front for 8 good seconds, then blows out every last bubble to get ready to stand. His chest drops, his face sinks deeper, and the stand turns into a scramble with a mouthful of pool. **Keep the air in until your feet are down**: if you feel yourself sinking just before you stand, you emptied the bags too early.
cards.simpler: Sam floats face down for 8 good seconds. Then, to get ready to stand, Sam blows out every last bubble. Sam's chest drops, the face sinks deeper, and the stand becomes a scramble with a mouthful of pool water. **Keep the air in until your feet are down.** If you feel yourself sinking just before you stand, you emptied the air bags too early.

cards.prompt: A friend watches you lie still on your back for 30 seconds and asks what's actually holding you up. What's the honest answer?

options.text: My legs, kicking very gently under the water
The air in my lungs, with the water doing the rest
Keeping every muscle tight so I stay flat

whyNot.a: That's kicking, which comes in chapter 5, not floating: today your legs did nothing.
whyNot.c: That's holding yourself up, not lying on the bed: tight muscles add no air, they just tire you out.

cards.reteach: Floating isn't something you do. It's something you stop fighting. The air in your chest is the float and the water holds the rest of you; your only jobs are keeping the air in and your head back.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body:
**Your lungs are air bags**: keep them mostly full and your chest stays at the surface, and lay your ears in the water so your hips come up too. To get up, chin to chest, knees in, hands press down, and keep the air until your feet are on the floor.

Tomorrow: why one push off the wall beats your first ten strokes.
cards.simpler: **Your lungs are air bags.** Keep them mostly full and your chest stays at the surface. Rest your ears in the water and your hips come up too. To get up, tuck your chin to your chest, pull your knees in, and press your hands down. Hold on to the air until your feet touch the floor. Tomorrow: why one push off the wall beats your first ten strokes.

cards.body: In the bath tonight, lie back with your ears under, take a full breath and feel your chest lift. Then sigh it all out and feel it settle. That's today's lesson in 20 seconds.
cards.simpler: Tonight in the bath, lie back with your ears under the water. Take a full breath and **feel your chest lift**. Then let it all out with a sigh and feel your chest settle back down. That's today's whole lesson in 20 seconds.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now float on your back and your front by keeping your lungs full and your head back, then stand up calmly from both.
